cards.title: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2

depth.text: Anthropic's new **AI models** are for **ambitious technical work**, from coding to science

Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 are the **same underlying model**: Fable is available to all users with cyber and biology safeguards, while organizations doing beneficial cybersecurity or biomedical research can apply for Mythos. Anthropic says they generate outputs up to **30% faster** than Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1; a team of 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents **formalized Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours** with minimal human intervention.

cards.camps: Two camps: some testers praise Fable 5.2’s speed and coding on ambitious work; others say it’s hard to distinguish from Opus 5.5 on ordinary coding and question whether the cost is worth it.

And Sonnet 5.5 sometimes makes me forget about Opus. - Fable is good, but you really have to push the ambition of your prompt in order to see proper separation from Opus 5.5. I…

We've been early testing Fable 5.2, and have been surprised by its coding ability. It was able to work with an esoteric 600k line fortran codebase to speed up some computational material science work for us by 36 times (!). Given that this could be done in 2 days, we've decided to open-source the results https://github.com/discovered-materials/dm_qe

Why Fable 5.2 and not 5.5? My hypothesis - OpenAI and Anthropic are locked in battle. Whoever takes a step, the other one mirrors. Based on this hypothesis, I think we can expect to see a new Astra model soon given the new Fable release. And it could be that Anthropic released Fable 5.2 and kept 5.5 in reserve, in case the new Astra model performs better than 5.2

I tried Fable 5.2 tonight, asking it for a code review of an in-browser machine vision project done by Opus 5.5 over the last 11 days. It used up my 5-hour token budget in half an hour and reported 7 serious bugs; if they're real, they're pretty bad. It's also suggesting that I take a different overall approach to parts of the problem. But that's just a first impression.

cards.title: Fable 5.2 one-shotted my nephew's dream game

depth.text: someone turned his nephew's drawings into a **fun beat-'em-up** with **AI**

Lex Toumbourou gave Claude **Fable 5.2** scans of the characters and a big wish list. It rewrote most of the code, generated roughly **175 images** and 140 audio clips, then used a bot to run through all twelve stages in a headless browser. The finished game had **12 levels, 18 characters and four-player play**.

cards.camps: Two camps: some call it an amazing outcome for the kids; others say “one-shot” glosses over the human prompting, playtesting and iteration.

comments.text: Growing up, games were such a scarce commodity that you'd really suck all the marrow out and spend hours beating your best times, looking for Easter eggs, or messing with custom maps and mods. There was a whole genre of gameplay around just exploiting physics bugs to jump a bit further. The other night I carelessly made an infinite runner game while watching TV and the feeling of sheer abundance…

I feel for kids growing up with LLMs like this. They will never impress a parent, teacher or peer with a simple “hello world” type text game, when the peer could generate a full multiplayer video game with a couple of prompts. The world has changed and we can never go back.

"one-shotting" is fun for a low (human) effort toy, but it's a mistake to get overly hung up on LLMs getting everything right on the first try, since a lot of that is the harness and the internal prompting that makes it burn extra tokens to test everything to get it in that one "shot" (ui turn). depth.text: Google introduced two **AI systems**: one to protect **sensitive data** and one for **huge amounts of context**

**TPU 8tx** is built on the same silicon as TPU 8t, with hardware security that keeps sensitive data isolated even while it’s being processed; Google says it delivers **up to 2x lower latency** than TPU 8t with a near-zero performance penalty. **TPU 8i Max** combines two TPU 8i chips on one package, doubling compute, SRAM and HBM bandwidth.

cards.title: CUI – Native UI components for C

cards.title: Starship Flight 15 on 11/13 plans to catch both booster and ship

depth.text: Starship Flight 15 plans to **catch** both the **booster** and **ship**

If successful, it would mark the **first full recovery** of an orbital launch system. The mission plan expects Starship to orbit Earth at **~275 km** and complete **approximately 14 orbits** over a more than 22-hour flight.

cards.camps: Two camps: one commenter says SpaceX’s focus is serving Elon and the share price, and argues for Earth-based clean-energy datacenters; another says Starship works and SpaceX has a huge lead, while acknowledging concern about quasi-monopolizing access to space.

cards.title: When a language's creator and its owners strongly disagree [pdf]

depth.text: C++'s creator and its **standards committee** disagree over whether **contracts** belong in the language

Bjarne Stroustrup's **opposition to contracts** may have tipped the scale in the failed **C++26 vote**, though commenters also point to broader fatigue with large, half-baked features like modules. Herb Sutter's summary lays out **six possible paths forward**, including removing contracts or voting again.

cards.camps: Two camps: some think Stroustrup's opposition may have tipped the vote; others say that overstates his role and misses wider weariness with half-baked features.

comments.text: Stroustrup's list of objections sounds quite sensible to me: https://www.stroustrup.com/Contracts_fundamental_flaws.pdf

I think this is putting too much weight on this event and Bjarne’s position on contracts. Bjarne’s opposition to contracts might have tipped the scale but there is definitely growing weariness (and wariness) about large half-baked features that are left as exercises to the implementors (looking at you modules). Ignoring that historical context when analysing this vote seems like a mistake.

This is a well-written and quite diplomatic summary by Herb Sutter. I'm not plugged in enough to be sure he's correct that Stroustrup's opposition was the main reason the C++26 vote failed where others have passed, but it sounds plausible. It also lists 6 possible paths forward for C++26 with pros and cons. I think they are roughly: A. Skip an official C++26 standard but roll these features into…
36 years of sustained agreement is not good; it means nobody is saying no to anything, and you have a giant, dirty snowball rolling down a mountain.

Just stopped by to say Sutter is not only right to be reiterating Bjarne's position here, he is also the author of IMO the most impactful paper regarding the progress of hardware performance and the shift to concurrent execution: https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~lin/cs380p/Free_Lunch.pdf

glossary.token: A chunk of text an AI reads or writes, often a whole word or part of one.
glossary.agent: An AI system that can take steps and use tools to get a task done, not just answer questions.
glossary.formalization: Writing mathematics in a precise form that a computer can check.
glossary.one-shot: A first version made from one prompt; it doesn't mean nobody changed the result afterward.
glossary.headless browser: A browser that runs under software control without a visible window.
glossary.spritesheet: An image that holds a game's character pictures, such as different poses or animation frames.
glossary.TPU: Thermoplastic polyurethane: a bendy kind of plastic used to make some printed parts.
glossary.silicon: The material used to make computer chips.
glossary.latency: The time between doing something and seeing the device respond.
glossary.context window: The amount of text and information an AI can take into account at one time.
glossary.SRAM: Static Random-Access Memory: a kind of memory that keeps its contents while powered, so the computer can use them quickly.
glossary.HBM: High-bandwidth memory: fast memory placed close to a processor so it can get lots of information quickly.
glossary.vibecoded: Made by asking an AI to write code from prompts, with little hands-on programming.
glossary.immediate mode: A way to build a UI where the app describes what should appear each time it draws, rather than keeping a lasting set of controls.
glossary.catch: A way to recover a rocket by having arms on the launch tower grab it when it returns.
glossary.booster: The lower part of a rocket that pushes it upward during launch.
glossary.orbital launch system: A rocket system meant to put a vehicle into a path around Earth.
glossary.inference: When an AI uses what it learned to answer or act, instead of being trained.
glossary.parameters: Learned values inside a model that shape the answers it gives.
glossary.compute-in-memory: A way to do calculations where the information is stored, avoiding moving it elsewhere first.
glossary.TOP/s: A measure of how many trillion calculations a chip can do each second.
glossary.contracts: Rules attached to code that say what should be true when it runs.
glossary.WG21: C++ Standardization Committee: the group that discusses and votes on proposed changes to C++.
glossary.modules: A way to divide C++ code into pieces that can be used separately.
